1.open: Think of someone who has led you well, like a coach, boss, teacher or neighbor. What made you trust them?
questions: Paul says his work is for "the faith of God's elect and their knowledge of the truth that leads to godliness" (v. 1). Why might he tie truth and the way we live so closely together?
Paul describes the hope of eternal life as something "God, who cannot lie, promised before time began" (v. 2). What does it mean to you that this hope rests on God's character and not on ours?
Paul left Titus in Crete to "set in order what was unfinished" (v. 5). Where have you seen a church, group or family struggle because no one was caring for the unfinished work?
Verses 6 to 8 describe a leader's home life, temper, money habits and welcome to guests. Why do you think Paul cares about everyday character this much, not only about knowledge or talent?

Verse 9 says a leader must "hold firmly to the faithful word" so that he can "encourage others by sound teaching." How have you been encouraged by someone who knew the Bible well and also cared about you?

Verse 7 warns against leaders who are "quick-tempered" or "greedy for money," and verse 11 says false teachers act for "dishonorable gain." How can we tell the difference between someone serving people and someone using them?
Verse 12 repeats a harsh saying about Cretans as a whole people. Many readers find it uncomfortable. How do you hear it, and what should we be careful about when we describe whole groups of people?

Verse 16 says some "profess to know God, but by their actions they deny Him." Where do you notice a gap between what you say you believe and how you live? What would honesty about that look like, even if you are not sure what you believe right now?
1.life: Pick one person who leads or teaches you, such as a pastor, boss or mentor. This week, thank them for something specific about how they live, and pray for them by name each day.
1.prayer: Thank God that his promises can be trusted because he cannot lie. Pray for the leaders and teachers in your church, and ask for a closer match between what you say you believe and how you live.
1.tip: Verses 6 to 9 raise questions about who may lead, and verses 12 to 16 sound harsh. Say plainly that Christians differ on the one-wife requirement and on whether elders and overseers are one role or two, then bring the group back to the main point: character and sound teaching both matter. For verse 12, name that it is a stereotype Paul quotes, and invite honest reactions without rushing to defend or condemn.

2.open: Who is someone older than you who taught you something useful, and what was it?
questions: Paul wants Titus to "speak the things that are consistent with sound doctrine" (v. 1). What does it look like when what someone believes and how they live actually match?
Older men and older women are given the job of setting an example, and older women are to be "teachers of good" (v. 3). Who has played that role in your life, and what did they do that made it work?

Verses 4 and 5 ask older women to train younger ones, and the stated reason is "so that the word of God will not be discredited" (v. 5). Why do you think Paul cares so much about how outsiders see the church?

Christians disagree about whether the instructions to wives are lasting commands or guidance shaped by the household customs of that time. How can your group talk about that honestly without anyone feeling pushed?
Paul tells Titus to "show yourself to be an example by doing good works" (v. 7). Where do you feel your life most clearly points people toward Jesus, and where does it get in the way?

Verses 9 and 10 tell enslaved believers to submit to their masters, and the letter does not speak against slavery itself. Many readers find that deeply troubling. What troubles you here, and what questions would you want to ask?
Verse 11 says "the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone." How does starting with grace change the way you read the instructions before it?

Verse 12 says grace "instructs us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions." What does it mean for grace to teach us, and not only forgive us? If you are not sure it works that way for you, say so.
2.life: Pick one person from a different age group than yours. Reach out this week to ask about their life, or to offer to help with something. Notice what you can learn from each other.
2.prayer: Thank God that his grace has "appeared" in Jesus for everyone (v. 11). Ask him to shape how you live so that others see something good about him. Pray for the people who have mentored you and for someone you might encourage.
2.tip: Verses 5 and 9 to 10 are the hard spots, and people may react strongly. Name the discomfort calmly, say plainly that Christians read these verses differently, and bring the group back to verses 11 to 14, where Paul gives his reason. Do not rush anyone to a tidy answer.

3.open: Think of a time someone showed you kindness you hadn't earned. What was it, and how did it feel?
questions: Paul asks believers "to malign no one, and to be peaceable and gentle, showing full consideration to everyone" (v. 2). Which of those is hardest for you, and when does it get hardest?
Paul says "at one time we too were foolish, disobedient, misled" (v. 3). Why might it help to remember our own past before we judge other people?
Verse 3 mentions being "enslaved to all sorts of desires and pleasures." What does that kind of slavery look like today, in ordinary life?
Verse 4 speaks of "the kindness of God our Savior and His love for mankind." When you picture God, is kindness the first word that comes to mind? What gets in the way, or helps?

Verse 5 says God saved us "not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy." How does it feel to hear that salvation is not earned? Be honest, even if it feels hard to believe or too easy.
Paul wants believers to "devote themselves to good deeds" (v. 8), and later to meet "the pressing needs of others" (v. 14). How are good deeds connected to grace, if they do not earn it?
Paul calls some arguments "pointless and worthless" (v. 9). How can we tell a question worth wrestling with from a quarrel that only divides people?
In verses 12 and 13, Paul asks the church to make sure Zenas and Apollos "have everything they need." Who around you has a practical need that your group could help meet?
3.life: Pick one person you tend to be impatient with or talk about unkindly. This week, remember how much kindness you have been given, and do one specific thing to show them gentleness or practical help.
3.prayer: Thank God for kindness we did not earn. Ask for the humility to remember our own story, and for the willingness to pass that kindness on to someone this week.
3.tip: Verse 5 mentions the "washing of new birth," and Christians differ on whether this means baptism itself brings new life or is an outward sign of what God does inwardly. Say so in a line, then steer back to the main point: salvation is God's gift, not our achievement. Also, verses 10 and 11 can sound harsh, so note they describe a patient process with two warnings, and are about persistent division, not honest doubt or hard questions.
